concepts.learning_objective: Distinguish final goods (consumption and capital goods, consumer durables) from intermediate goods by their economic use.
Distinguish stock variables, defined at a point of time, from flow variables, defined over a period of time.
Relate gross investment, depreciation and net investment, and explain the time trade-off between capital and consumer goods.
Identify the four factors of production and their remunerations: wage, interest, profit and rent.
Explain the circular flow of income and goods between households and firms in a simple economy.
Explain why the product, expenditure and income methods measure the same aggregate at different points of the circular flow.

topics.title: The product or value added method

concepts.learning_objective: Calculate value added and explain how deducting intermediate goods avoids double counting.
Calculate gross and net value added, using change in inventories and depreciation.
Distinguish inventory (a stock) from change in inventories (a flow), and planned from unplanned changes.
Compute GDP as C + I + G + X - M and explain the treatment of intermediate goods and imports.
Compute GDP as the sum of wages, profits, interest and rent, and verify it against value added.

topics.title: Factor cost, basic prices and market prices

concepts.learning_objective: Distinguish production taxes and subsidies from product taxes and subsidies with examples.
Convert GVA between factor cost, basic prices and market prices using net production and net product taxes.
Derive GNP, NNP at market prices and National Income (NNP at factor cost) from GDP.
Derive Personal Income and Personal Disposable Income from National Income.
Calculate National Disposable Income and identify the components of Private Income.

topics.title: Nominal and real GDP and price indices

concepts.learning_objective: Distinguish nominal GDP at current prices from real GDP at constant base-year prices.
Calculate the GDP (or GNP) deflator and interpret what it says about the price level.
Calculate a Consumer Price Index and explain how CPI and WPI differ from the GDP deflator.
Evaluate why a rise in GDP may not raise welfare when its distribution is unequal.
Explain how non-monetary exchanges lead to underestimation of GDP.
Explain how negative and positive externalities make GDP misstate welfare.
